title: Social Interaction Breaks Replicate Independence in Controlled-Clone LLM Agents
claim: Identical clones with fixed private briefs diverge in off-topic responses when they interact, but not when kept isolated.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right, shared clone source and bracketed outputs
description: A left-to-right experimental design diagram. A network-icon box labeled "Clones" on the far left splits via brackets into two identical rows of agents, each carrying document icons for private briefs. The top gray panel, "Interaction", shows blue, dark-blue, orange and brown agents with speech bubbles and colored double arrows between them, plus a "30 rounds" stopwatch. The bottom panel, "No Interaction", shows the same agents sitting isolated with no arrows, and a thick arrow runs along its bottom edge. Both panels have small graph-document icons at the corners. On the right, brackets lead to survey-checklist icons and dot-line matching diagrams. The top panel's lines are crossed and the bottom panel's are mostly straight. A vertical "Response Drift" label spans both outputs. The eye goes first to the large bold titles and the colorful agents.
caption: Interaction moves clones: same briefs, with or without 30 rounds.
abstract: Multi-agent LLM evaluations and social simulations create many agents from one model and treat them as independent replicates, even after the agents interact. This assumption remains untested with matched controls. We introduce SocCogEval, a controlled-clone assay for Social Cognitive Transfer (SCT). Clones share the base model, system prompt, and decoding parameters and differ only in a private brief, and a factorial protocol separates the brief, 30 rounds of interaction, and initialization noise. On Qwen3-122B-FP8, interaction with the briefs held fixed raises off-topic BFI-10 response-profile drift by $\barÎ=+0.917$ and $+0.912$ in two topically disjoint scenarios (exact $p=0.0008$ and $0.0039$). The drift is larger than under the brief alone, persists under temperature-zero re-probing, and stays positive without typed memory extraction in exploratory tests. Matched solo generation reproduces part of it, and social interaction remains highest. Across five more model variants, every scenario-averaged interaction contrast is positive. Each interacting population is therefore one replicate, and treating its agents as independent requires paired no-interaction controls.
